title: From the Hijrah to Ashura
intro: Ten days from the Islamic New Year to Ashura: the Hijrah, then the story of the Prophet Musa (Moses).

posts.display: When they two were in the cave, when he said unto his comrade: Grieve not. Lo! Allah is with us.
posts.display_original: إِذْ هُمَا فِى ٱلْغَارِ إِذْ يَقُولُ لِصَٰحِبِهِۦ لَا تَحْزَنْ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ مَعَنَا
posts.caption: For many Muslims, the Islamic year 1449 begins around now with the month of Muharram. The calendar counts its years from the Hijrah, the migration of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ from Mecca to Medina in 622 CE. On the way, he and his companion Abu Bakr hid in a cave while their pursuers searched nearby. His words to his worried friend, "Grieve not. Lo! Allah is with us", are remembered as a model of calm trust in danger.

Over the coming days: the story of the Prophet Musa (Moses), leading to Ashura on the tenth of Muharram. For Shia Muslims, these ten days are also a time of mourning for Husayn ibn Ali. When Pharaoh was killing the Israelites' newborn sons, Musa's mother set her baby adrift on the river. Pharaoh's household found him, but he refused every nurse until his sister led them to his own mother. The verse draws the lesson: Allah's promise is true.

Grown up, Musa had to flee Egypt alone, a migration of his own long before the Hijrah. A blow he struck to defend an Israelite had killed an Egyptian; he asked Allah's forgiveness, but the chiefs plotted to kill him. He set out with no plan except hope in his Lord's guidance; Pickthall's "peradventure" means perhaps. In Midian he found a home, work and a family.

posts.display: And when he reached it, he was called from the right side of the valley in the blessed field, from the tree: O Moses! Lo! I, even I, am Allah, the Lord of the Worlds.
posts.caption: Years later, travelling with his family, Musa saw a fire on the mountainside and went toward it, hoping for news or a burning brand to warm them. Instead, by a tree in a blessed valley near Mount Sinai, he was called by name. This is the moment he became a prophet.

Sent to Pharaoh, Musa asks for his brother Harun (Aaron) to share the task. Pickthall's "henchman" simply translates wazir, a helper or minister. Notice the reason Musa gives: not power or safety, but that together they may glorify and remember Allah more.

Musa and Harun admit their fear that Pharaoh will act hastily or tyrannically. The reply is short: do not fear, I am with you both, hearing and seeing. It echoes the words of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ in the cave during the Hijrah: "Allah is with us".

In Ash-Shu'ara, Musa and Harun go together to Pharaoh, the most powerful ruler of their world, with a message from the Lord of the Worlds and a plain demand: let the Children of Israel go. Commentators see in it the courage to speak truth to a tyrant, though Surah Ta-Ha adds that they were told to speak to him "a gentle word". In the next verse, Pharaoh answers by reminding Musa that he had grown up in Pharaoh's own house.

Pharaoh summoned his best magicians to defeat Musa. When Musa's staff swallowed their illusions, they recognized something beyond magic and fell down in prostration. In the verses that follow they hold to their new faith even under Pharaoh's threats. Pickthall's "wizards" means sorcerers or magicians.

After years of signs and warnings, Musa is told to lead the Children of Israel out of Egypt by night. The promise is a dry path through the sea, with no need to fear being overtaken. Pickthall's "My slaves" means Allah's servants. Ashura, the tenth of Muharram, is close.

For many Muslims, Ashura, the tenth of Muharram, falls around now. With Pharaoh's army behind them and the sea ahead, Musa's people panic, and he answers with complete trust. Many Sunni Muslims fast on Ashura in remembrance of Musa's deliverance, while Shia Muslims mourn the martyrdom of Husayn ibn Ali, grandson of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, at Karbala (680 CE).
